subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
subtype: Approach: apologising and offering repair to the client [Action]
passage:
The call was set for ten o'clock in the Andheri office. Lokesh, the manager, sat beside Devika, and Devika held the notes she'd written the night before.
"Mr Sen, our export ran twice and your last invoice showed double the amount," Devika said. "It was our mistake. We have already corrected it. Your account will be right by Friday, and you'll receive a written summary tomorrow."
There was a pause. Then Lokesh added, "We're also giving you one month's fee as credit."
Mr Sen said, "Thank you for not making excuses. Send me the summary."
Devika ended the call, exhaled and only then noticed her palms were damp. Lokesh gave a small nod and said, "Well said. That was clear."

qa.q: By which day will Mr Sen's account be correct?
qa.a: It will be right by Friday.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling before and during the call?
qa.a: Devika was nervous, with damp palms, but spoke clearly from her notes.

qa.q: What could Devika and Lokesh do after the call to keep Mr Sen's trust?
qa.a: They could send the written summary on time and check with Mr Sen after Friday that the invoice is correct.

qa.q: How might Mr Sen have felt hearing the explanation?
qa.a: Mr Sen appreciated the plain explanation without excuses, and probably felt reassured by the timeline and the credit.

grounding: The passage shows a manager and employee calling an affected client, explaining plainly, sharing a recovery timeline and offering a service credit.

subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
subtype: Approach: apologising and offering repair to the client [Action]
passage:
'Mr Rao, thank you for taking the call,' Seema said. Saurabh sat beside her, notes in hand.
'I've been waiting two days for an explanation,' the client said.
'You'll have it now. Saurabh?'
Saurabh took a breath. 'On Tuesday I applied an update that broke the order export. Your team couldn't download orders for nineteen hours. That was my mistake, not a system glitch.'
Silence. Then, 'Go on.'
'The export works again as of this morning. By Friday we'll have re-sent every missed order file, and we've added a check so no update can go live unless the export test passes.'
Seema added, 'We're also giving you a service credit for this month. Not as a favour, as a fair repair.'
Mr Rao exhaled. 'Honestly, I expected excuses. This is better.'

qa.q: How long couldn't the client's team download orders?
What might Saurabh have been feeling on taking a breath?
qa.a: Saurabh was probably nervous and a little ashamed, bracing to admit the mistake plainly to an upset client.

qa.q: What would make the repair even stronger after this call?
qa.a: Sending Mr Rao a short written summary of the cause, the timeline and the new check, and following up on Friday as promised.

qa.q: How does the call look to Mr Rao?
qa.a: Mr Rao expected excuses, so a plain admission, a timeline and a credit make him more willing to trust the team.

grounding: It shows a manager and employee calling the client to explain the issue plainly, share recovery timelines and offer a service credit instead of excuses.

subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
subtype: Approach: apologising and offering repair to the client [Action]
passage:
I'm Vasudha, and the call I dreaded most last year turned out to be the one I'm proudest of. I had sent the wrong batch of payslips to a client company: three hundred employees got a colleague's salary details. I wanted to write a long email full of 'technical issues'. My manager, Pallavi, said, 'No. We call them. Today.'
So we did. I said it myself: 'I attached the wrong file. It was my error.' Pallavi explained how we had recalled the email, which staff had opened it and what we would tell them. We gave dates: correct payslips by Thursday, a privacy review by the following week. Then she offered two months of service at no charge.
The client's HR head was silent for a long moment, then said, 'Thank you for not hiding it.' They renewed with us in March.

qa.q: How many employees got a colleague's salary details?
How does Vasudha feel about that call now?
qa.a: Vasudha feels proud of it, even though at the time Vasudha dreaded it and wanted to hide behind 'technical issues'.

qa.q: What other approach did Vasudha first want, and why was the call better?
qa.a: A long email blaming 'technical issues'; the call was better because owning the error and giving dates made the client trust the repair.

qa.q: How might the client's HR head have experienced the call?
qa.a: Facing upset staff, the HR head was likely angry at first but relieved that the firm owned the mistake and had a plan.

grounding: It shows an employee and manager calling the affected client, explaining plainly, sharing recovery dates and offering a service credit, which rebuilds credibility.
